what-is-terminal.title: What is a Terminal?
what-is-terminal.description: Learn what a terminal is and how it works on Android. This is the foundation for everything else you'll learn. You'll discover how typing commands replaces clicking buttons, and how Termux turns your phone into a mini Linux environment.

items.title: What is a Terminal?
items.content:
A terminal is a text-based interface for controlling your computer. Instead of clicking buttons with a mouse, you type commands. When you press Enter, the computer executes your command.

Termux brings this same experience to Android. It turns your phone into a mini Linux environment where you can run real commands, install software, write code, and automate tasks — all from a simple text interface.

Think of it this way: while most apps have buttons and menus, Termux is like having a conversation with your phone by typing instructions. It's more powerful but requires learning a few key concepts.

The terminal doesn't have graphics, icons, or mouse support. Everything is text-based. This makes it incredibly fast and powerful once you learn the basics.
items.exercise: Open Termux and type the word 'hello'. What do you see? Then try typing 'pwd' and see what happens. Notice how the terminal responds to each command you type.

items.title: Your First Command
items.content:
Before installing anything, you need to update Termux's list of available apps. This is like refreshing a webpage to get the latest content.

The command you'll run is pkg update. pkg is Termux's package manager — it handles installing and updating software. update tells it to refresh its list of available packages from the internet.

When you run this, you'll see a lot of text scroll by. This is normal! Termux is downloading the latest information about what software is available to install.

After the update completes, you should also run pkg upgrade to install any updates to your existing software. This keeps everything secure and working properly.
items.exercise: Run pkg update and watch what happens. Notice how it fetches the latest package lists from the internet. Then run pkg upgrade to install any updates. Pay attention to what gets updated.

items.title: Understanding the Prompt
items.content:
The text before your cursor tells you where you are in the file system. This is called the 'prompt' and it's your guide to navigation.

In Termux, the prompt typically shows your current folder followed by a symbol. ~ means you're in your home folder. $ means you're a regular user (not root).

When you navigate to different folders, the prompt updates to show your new location. This helps you stay oriented as you move around the file system.

Your home folder (represented by ~) is where all your personal files and projects should live. It's your safe space within the file system.
items.exercise: Type pwd to see your current location. Then type cd / and pwd again. What changed? Try cd ~ to go back home. Notice how the prompt changes to show your location.

how-commands-work.title: How Commands Work
how-commands-work.description: Understand the pattern behind every terminal command. Commands follow a simple structure that once you learn, you can use any terminal on any system. This section breaks down the command pattern and teaches you to navigate like a pro.

items.title: The Command Pattern
items.content:
Every terminal command follows a simple pattern: COMMAND followed by WHAT TO ACT ON. This is like giving instructions: first the action (verb), then the target (noun).

For example, ls Documents means 'list the contents of the Documents folder'. cp file.txt backup/ means 'copy file.txt to the backup folder'.

Some commands don't need a target. ls by itself lists the current folder. pwd shows where you are without needing any extra information.

Understanding this pattern makes learning new commands much easier. You'll find that most commands follow this same structure.
items.exercise: Try running ls with different folders. For example: ls /data or ls ~/storage. What do you see? Notice how the output changes based on the folder you specify.

items.title: Step-by-Step: Navigate Folders
items.content:
Navigation is the most important skill in the terminal. You'll constantly move between folders, check where you are, and see what's inside.

The three essential navigation commands are: pwd (where am I?), ls (what's here?), and cd (go there). Master these and you can navigate anywhere.

When you use cd, you can go to a folder by name, go up one level with cd .., or go to your home folder with cd ~.

The cd .. command is particularly useful — it takes you to the parent folder of your current location. Use it to go back up the folder structure.
items.exercise: Create a folder called 'myfiles' using mkdir myfiles. Navigate into it with cd myfiles, then create another folder inside called 'docs' with mkdir docs. Use pwd and ls to verify each step. Then use cd .. to go back up one level.

items.title: Making Your First File
items.content:
Creating and editing files is essential. You'll start with simple text files using the Nano editor, which is beginner-friendly.

Nano is a simple text editor that runs in the terminal. It shows you what you're typing and has basic commands at the bottom of the screen. The most important shortcuts are: Ctrl+O to save and Ctrl+X to exit.

When you create a file with touch, it's empty. When you use nano, you can actually type content into it. This is how you'll write notes, scripts, and code.

Nano has a learning curve but it's the simplest editor to start with. The commands are shown at the bottom of the screen while you're using it.
items.exercise: Create a file called 'journal.txt' using touch journal.txt. Then open it with nano journal.txt. Write today's date and a short note about what you're learning. Save it with Ctrl+O, press Enter to confirm, and exit with Ctrl+X. Then view your file with cat journal.txt.

essential-commands.title: Essential Commands
essential-commands.description: The most important commands you'll use every day. These are your bread and butter — memorize them and you'll be able to navigate any terminal environment with confidence.

items.title: The Three Most Important Commands
items.content:
Memorize these three commands. You will use them constantly in your terminal journey. They are your navigation tools.

ls tells you what's in the current folder. cd moves you to a different folder. pwd tells you exactly where you are.

When you're lost or confused, use these three commands to reorient yourself. pwd shows where you are, ls shows what's around you, and cd takes you where you want to go.

The ls command can be enhanced with options like -l for detailed view or -a to show hidden files. These make it even more useful.
items.exercise: Practice navigating: Go to your home folder with cd ~, list what's there with ls, go into a folder with cd foldername, check your location with pwd, and come back with cd .. or cd ~. Do this 5 times until it's automatic.

items.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
items.content:
Everyone makes mistakes when learning the terminal. Don't feel bad when you see errors — they're part of the learning process.

The most common mistakes are forgetting spaces (commands need spaces between parts), wrong capitalization (Linux is case-sensitive), and typos.

Error messages might look scary but they usually tell you exactly what went wrong. command not found means you typed something that doesn't exist. No such file or directory means the file or folder you mentioned doesn't exist where you are.

Learning to read error messages is a valuable skill. They often contain the exact information you need to fix the problem.
items.exercise: Try making each mistake on purpose: type pwdDocuments (no space), type Ls (capital L), type delet file.txt (wrong command). See what each error message says. Understanding error messages is a superpower!

items.title: Getting Help
items.content:
When you're stuck, Termux has built-in help systems. You don't need to memorize everything.

Most commands have a --help option that shows a quick reference. For more detailed information, you can use the man (manual) command.

You can also use the history command to see what you've typed before and re-run commands with !number.

The man pages are comprehensive but sometimes overwhelming. Start with --help for quick reference, then use man for deeper understanding.
items.exercise: Try ls --help and scroll through the options. Then install man with pkg install man and read the manual for pwd with man pwd. Press Q to exit the manual. Then try history to see your command history.

mini-project.title: Mini Project
mini-project.description: Put everything together in a real project. This is where you'll apply all the commands you've learned in a practical scenario, building confidence through hands-on practice.

items.title: Your First Mini Project: A Journal
items.content:
Now you'll put everything together. Create a daily journal to practice all the commands you've learned.

This project uses: mkdir to create folders, cd to navigate, nano to write, cat to read, cp to backup, and ls to check your work.

Start by creating a journal folder, then write your first entry. Make a backup copy to practice the cp command. Finally, use ls -la to see all the details of your files.

This workflow mirrors what developers do every day: creating files, editing them, backing them up, and checking their work.
items.exercise: Create a journal folder with mkdir journal. Navigate into it with cd journal. Create today's entry with nano 2026-04-08.txt. Write your entry, save with Ctrl+O, exit with Ctrl+X. Read it with cat. Make a backup with cp 2026-04-08.txt backup.txt. See all entries with ls -la.

items.title: What To Do Next
items.content:
Congratulations! You've completed the beginner guide. Here's your path forward to becoming a terminal power user.

You've learned: what a terminal is, how to read the prompt, navigation with pwd/ls/cd, file operations like touch/nano/cat/cp, and how to get help.

Now it's time to explore the main course where you'll learn about package management, Git, Python, networking, and much more.

Remember: the terminal is a skill that improves with practice. Keep using it daily and you'll become more comfortable and efficient.
items.exercise: Create a folder called 'challenge' with mkdir challenge. Inside it, create a file called 'done.txt' with the text 'I completed the beginner guide!' using echo. Make a backup copy called 'done_backup.txt' with cp. List everything with details using ls -la. You've now used mkdir, cd, echo, cp, and ls -la.

getting-started.title: Getting Started
getting-started.description: Install and set up Termux properly on your device. This section covers everything from downloading the right version to verifying your installation works correctly.

items.title: Where to Download Termux
items.content:
The Google Play Store version is abandoned and broken. Always use the F-Droid version for the best experience with regular updates.

F-Droid is an open-source app store that provides the official, maintained version of Termux. The Play Store version was abandoned by the developers and is severely outdated.

After installing from F-Droid, open the app and wait. The first launch takes 10-30 seconds to set up the environment.

Installing from F-Droid also gives you access to the latest features and security updates that the Play Store version lacks.
items.exercise: Go to F-Droid on your device, search for Termux, and check the version number. Make sure you're running the latest version. If you have the Play Store version, uninstall it and install from F-Droid.

items.title: First Launch and Initial Setup
items.content:
When Termux first opens, you'll see a black screen with white text and a $ symbol. This is your terminal prompt — it means Termux is ready for your commands.

The first thing you should do is update everything. This ensures you have the latest package list and all software is up to date.

Run pkg update first to refresh the package list, then pkg upgrade to install any updates. When prompted 'Do you want to continue?', type Y and press Enter.

This two-step process is essential. It ensures your Termux environment is current and secure.
items.exercise: Run pkg update and watch how it fetches the latest package lists. Then run pkg upgrade and observe what gets updated. This is the first thing you should do every time you open Termux.

items.title: Grant Storage Access
items.content:
Termux needs permission to see your Android files like photos, downloads, and documents. This is essential for working with your phone's files.

Run the termux-setup-storage command. Termux will ask for permission to access your storage. Tap 'Allow'.

After this, you'll have access to your Android storage at ~/storage/shared/. This folder is a link to your phone's internal storage.

Without this step, you won't be able to access your Android files from Termux, which limits what you can do.
items.exercise: Run termux-setup-storage and grant permission when prompted. Then navigate to your Downloads folder using cd ~/storage/shared/Downloads. List the files there with ls. You should see your downloaded files.

items.title: Verify Everything Works
items.content:
Run these tests to confirm your Termux installation is working correctly. This will catch any issues early.

Test 1 checks that the package manager works. Test 2 verifies storage access. Test 3 confirms you can create and read files. Test 4 checks your internet connection.

If all tests pass, your Termux is ready for serious work. If any fail, go back and troubleshoot the specific issue.

These tests are quick and give you confidence that everything is set up properly.
items.exercise: Run all four test commands: pkg --version to check the version, ls ~/storage/shared/ to check storage, echo 'Termux is working' > test.txt and cat test.txt to test file creation, and ping -c 2 google.com to test connectivity. If all pass, your Termux is ready!

items.title: Understanding Termux Storage
items.content:
Termux has its own private storage separate from Android. This is for security — other apps can't see your Termux files by default.

Your Termux home folder is at /data/data/com.termux/files/home/. This is private to Termux. Other apps on your phone cannot access this folder.

To share files with other apps, you need to copy them to the shared storage at ~/storage/shared/. This folder is accessible by both Termux and Android apps.

Understanding this separation is important for organizing your files and keeping sensitive data secure.
items.exercise: Create a file in Termux with echo 'Hello Termux' > private.txt. Then copy it to your Android Documents folder with cp private.txt ~/storage/shared/Documents/. Verify it appears there using a file explorer app on your phone.

basic-commands.title: Basic Commands
basic-commands.description: Master the fundamental commands for file management and navigation. These are the commands you'll use every single day, so getting comfortable with them is essential.

items.title: pwd - Where Am I?
items.content:
pwd stands for Print Working Directory. It shows your exact location in the file system.

Use this command whenever you feel lost. It tells you exactly which folder you're in. This is especially useful when you've been navigating through multiple folders.

If you ever get completely lost, type cd ~ to go to your home folder, then pwd to confirm you're back home.

The output of pwd is a full path starting from the root of the file system, which helps you understand exactly where you are.
items.exercise: Navigate to different folders and run pwd each time. Start in your home folder, go to /data, go to ~/storage, and run pwd at each location. See how the output changes to show your current location.

items.title: ls - What Is Here?
items.content:
ls lists all files and folders in your current location. Use it to explore and see what you're working with.

By itself, ls shows just the names. Add -l for a detailed list with permissions, size, and date. Add -a to show hidden files (files starting with a dot).

You can also combine flags: ls -la shows everything in long format with hidden files included.

The ls command is your primary tool for exploring the file system and understanding what's in each folder.
items.exercise: Create some files and folders: touch file1.txt file2.txt and mkdir testfolder. Then use ls with different flags: ls (basic), ls -l (detailed), ls -a (including hidden), and ls -la (all details). Notice how the output changes with each flag.

items.title: cd - Go There
items.content:
cd stands for Change Directory. It moves you into different folders. It's how you navigate the file system.

Use cd folder_name to go into a folder. Use cd .. to go up one level (to the parent folder). cd ~ takes you to your home folder from anywhere.

Tab completion is a great time-saver: type cd Docu and press Tab — it will auto-complete to cd Documents/ if that folder exists.

The cd command is how you move around the file system. Combined with pwd and ls, you can explore any part of your device.
items.exercise: Practice navigating: go to root with cd /, then to your home with cd ~, then to a subfolder. Use pwd to verify each step. Try using Tab completion to navigate to folders faster.

items.title: mkdir - Create Folders
items.content:
mkdir stands for Make Directory. It creates new folders to organize your files.

Always use lowercase names without spaces for compatibility. Use underscores or hyphens instead of spaces: my_folder or my-folder.

You can create multiple folders at once by listing them all after the command.

Organizing your files into folders is essential for keeping your work tidy and easy to find.
items.exercise: Create a folder structure: mkdir projects and then mkdir projects/python projects/web projects/data. Use ls -R projects to see the nested structure. Then create multiple folders at once with mkdir folder1 folder2 folder3.

items.title: touch - Create Empty Files
items.content:
touch creates an empty file. It's also used to update a file's timestamp to the current time.

If the file doesn't exist, touch creates it. If it already exists, touch updates its modification time without changing the content.

You can create multiple files at once by listing all their names.

touch is useful for creating placeholder files or updating timestamps for build systems and scripts.
items.exercise: Create several empty files: touch file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt. Then use ls -l to see their timestamps. Use touch again on one file to update its timestamp: touch file1.txt. Check ls -l again to see the timestamp change.

items.title: cat - Read Files
items.content:
cat displays the entire contents of a file. It's great for small files but can overwhelm your screen for large ones.

For large files, use less to scroll through page by page, head to see the first few lines, or tail to see the last few lines.

cat can also combine multiple files: cat file1.txt file2.txt shows both one after another.

Understanding the limitations of cat helps you choose the right tool for viewing files.
items.exercise: Create a file with 20 lines of text. Use cat to view it all, then use head -5 to see the first 5 lines, and tail -5 to see the last 5 lines. Notice how each command shows different parts of the file.

items.title: cp - Copy Files
items.content:
cp stands for Copy. It creates a copy of a file or folder. The original remains unchanged, and you get a duplicate.

To copy a folder and everything inside it, use -r (recursive). To preserve timestamps and permissions, use -p.

Copying is safe — it never changes the original file. Use it for backups or creating new versions.

cp is one of the most frequently used commands. Mastering it is essential for managing files.
items.exercise: Create a file with echo 'Hello' > original.txt. Copy it to a new name with cp original.txt copy.txt. Then copy it to a different folder with cp original.txt ~/storage/shared/Documents/. Verify both copies exist with ls.

items.title: mv - Move or Rename
items.content:
mv stands for Move. It moves files to different locations OR renames them. Unlike cp, no copy is created — the file actually moves.

When you use mv to rename a file, it stays in the same folder but gets a new name. When you use it to move a file, it goes to a different folder.

The difference from cp: cp makes a duplicate, mv actually moves the file (no copy remains in the original location).
items.exercise: Create a file with echo 'Test' > file.txt. Rename it with mv file.txt renamed.txt. Then move it to a different folder with mkdir testfolder && mv renamed.txt testfolder/. Use ls to verify the original location is now empty and ls testfolder/ to see the file in the new location.

items.title: rm - Delete Files
items.content:
rm stands for Remove. It permanently deletes files. There is NO undo — be very careful with this command.

Always use -i (interactive) when learning — it asks for confirmation before deleting each file. Use ls first to see what you're deleting before running rm.

Never run rm -rf / — this would delete everything in Termux. Be extremely careful with recursive deletion (-r) and force (-f) flags.

The rm command is powerful but dangerous. Always double-check what you're deleting.
items.exercise: Create several test files with touch test1.txt test2.txt test3.txt. Use rm -i test1.txt to delete with confirmation. Then delete all remaining files with rm *.txt. Notice how the -i flag asks for confirmation before each deletion.

package-management.title: Package Management
package-management.description: Learn to install and manage software packages on Termux. Package management is how you get new tools and keep everything up to date.

items.title: What is a Package Manager?
items.content:
A package manager is like an app store for the command line. It downloads, installs, and manages software automatically.

Termux uses pkg as its package manager. When you tell it what to install, it handles everything: finding the software, downloading it, installing dependencies, and setting it up correctly.

The benefits are huge: automatic dependency handling, easy updates for all software, clean uninstallation, and verified safe packages from trusted repositories.

Without a package manager, you'd have to manually find, download, and install each piece of software and its dependencies.
items.exercise: Search for Python packages using pkg search python. Install a small package like nano if you don't have it with pkg install nano. Then check what's installed with pkg list-installed.

items.title: Essential pkg Commands
items.content:
These are the only pkg commands you need to know. Memorize them and you can manage any package.

Always start with pkg update to refresh the list of available packages, then pkg upgrade to install updates. This should be your first action whenever you open Termux.

Use pkg search to find packages, pkg install to install them, and pkg uninstall to remove them.

The pkg clean command removes downloaded package files, which frees up space on your device.
items.exercise: Practice the full package cycle: pkg update to refresh, pkg search htop to find it, pkg install htop to install it, htop to run it (press Q to quit), pkg uninstall htop to remove it, and pkg clean to clean up. This is the complete package management workflow.

items.title: Must-Have Packages
items.content:
These packages are essential for any Termux user. Install them to unlock the full potential of your terminal.

Text editors: nano (simple, beginner-friendly) and vim (powerful, steeper learning curve). File downloading: wget and curl. Programming: python and nodejs. Version control: git. System access: openssh for remote connections. Utilities: tree for folder visualization, htop for task management, man for manual pages.

These packages will give you a complete development environment on your phone.
items.exercise: Install tree and use it to visualize your folder structure: tree ~/. Then install htop and run it to see your system processes (press Q to quit). Then install man and read the manual for ls: man ls (press Q to quit).

items.title: Repository Management
items.content:
Packages come from repositories. You can change mirrors if downloads are slow or add extra repositories for more software.

Termux has several repositories: main (primary), root (for rooted devices), x11 (graphical applications), and game (games).

Use termux-change-repo to switch to a faster mirror if downloads are slow. Use arrow keys to navigate, Space to select, Enter to confirm.

Changing repositories can significantly improve download speeds depending on your location.
items.exercise: Run termux-change-repo to see the available mirrors. You don't need to change anything, just explore the options. Then check your current repositories with cat $PREFIX/etc/apt/sources.list.

file-system.title: File System
file-system.description: Understand the Termux file system structure and paths. Knowing where things are and how paths work is essential for effective navigation and file management.

items.title: Termux Directory Structure
items.content:
Termux has its own isolated file system. Understanding where things are helps you navigate efficiently.

Your home folder (~) is where all your personal files and projects should go. This is the default location when you open Termux.

The packages folder ($PREFIX) is where installed software lives. You rarely need to touch this.

After running termux-setup-storage, you can access your Android storage at ~/storage/shared/.

Each folder serves a specific purpose. Keeping your files organized helps you work more efficiently.
items.exercise: Navigate to each of these folders and use ls to see what's inside: cd ~ (home), cd /data/data/com.termux/files/usr (packages), and cd ~/storage/shared/ (Android storage). Explore your Android storage folders like Downloads and DCIM.

items.title: Absolute vs Relative Paths
items.content:
Paths tell the computer where a file is. Understanding the difference is crucial for navigating efficiently.

An absolute path starts from the root (/) and works no matter where you are. Example: /data/data/com.termux/files/home/practice/mynote.txt

A relative path starts from your current location. Example: practice/mynote.txt (only works if you're in the home folder).

Special shortcuts: . (current folder), .. (parent folder), ~ (home folder), - (previous folder).
items.exercise: Practice using absolute and relative paths. Navigate to a folder using both methods: cd /data/data/com.termux/files/home (absolute) and cd ~ (relative with shortcut). Use pwd to verify your location each time.

storage-access.title: Storage Access
storage-access.description: Access and manage files on your Android device from Termux. This section covers setting up storage access and working with Android files.

items.title: Setting Up Storage Access
items.content:
Before you can access your Android files, you need to run termux-setup-storage. This command requests permission to access your phone's storage.

After you grant permission, you'll have access to your Android storage through ~/storage/. You'll see folders like shared/, downloads/, dcim/, pictures/, music/, and movies/.

If storage doesn't work properly, try removing the storage folder and setting it up again with rm -rf ~/storage && termux-setup-storage.

This setup only needs to be done once unless you reinstall Termux or revoke permissions.
items.exercise: Run termux-setup-storage and grant permission when prompted. Then navigate to your Downloads folder with cd ~/storage/shared/Downloads and list the files with ls. This confirms storage access is working.

items.title: Accessing Android Folders
items.content:
After setup, your Android storage is accessible through ~/storage/. Each folder maps to a different part of your Android storage.

~/storage/shared/ is the root of your internal storage — where you see all your files. The shortcuts like downloads/, dcim/, pictures/, music/, movies/, and documents/ give you quick access to specific folders.

You can navigate to these folders, list files, copy, move, and delete files just like any other folder in Termux.

These shortcuts make it easy to work with your Android files without having to remember complex paths.
items.exercise: Navigate to your Downloads folder with cd ~/storage/shared/Downloads and list the files with ls. Copy a file from there to your Termux home folder with cp filename.txt ~/. Then navigate to your DCIM folder with cd ~/storage/shared/DCIM/Camera and list the photos there.

items.title: Moving Files Between Environments
items.content:
Termux private storage and Android shared storage are separate. You need to explicitly copy or move files between them.

To copy from Termux to Android: cp ~/file.txt ~/storage/shared/Documents/

To copy from Android to Termux: cp ~/storage/shared/Download/document.pdf ~/

Use -r to copy entire folders (recursive). Use mv instead of cp if you want to move (rather than copy) the file.

Understanding how to move files between these environments is essential for sharing work with other apps.
items.exercise: Create a file in Termux with echo 'Hello' > myfile.txt. Copy it to your Android Documents folder with cp myfile.txt ~/storage/shared/Documents/. Verify it appears there with ls ~/storage/shared/Documents/. Then move a file from Android to Termux with mv ~/storage/shared/Download/somefile.pdf ~/.

items.title: Working with External SD Cards
items.content:
If your device has an SD card, you can access it from Termux. The location varies by device.

Common SD card mount points are /storage/sdcard1/ or /storage/XXXX-XXXX/ (where XXXX is a long alphanumeric string).

You can create a symlink for easier access: ln -s /storage/sdcard1 ~/sdcard. Then you can just use cd ~/sdcard to access your SD card.

Symlinks make it much easier to work with external storage because you don't have to remember the full path.
items.exercise: Check if you have an SD card mounted by looking in /storage/ with ls /storage/. If you find an SD card folder, create a symlink with ln -s /storage/sdcard1 ~/sdcard (replace sdcard1 with the actual folder name). Then navigate to it with cd ~/sdcard and list its contents with ls.

git-github.title: Git & GitHub
git-github.description: Learn version control with Git and collaborate on GitHub. Git is essential for any developer, and GitHub is where you'll share your work with the world.

items.title: Installing and Configuring Git
items.content:
Git tracks changes to files. Think of it as an unlimited undo button for your code and documents.

First, install Git with pkg install git. Then configure your identity with git config --global user.name and git config --global user.email. This information is attached to every commit you make.

Set your default editor to nano with git config --global core.editor 'nano' for an easier experience.

Git configuration only needs to be done once. After that, Git will remember your settings for all future projects.
items.exercise: Install Git with pkg install git. Configure your name and email with git config --global user.name 'Your Name' and git config --global user.email 'your@email.com'. Then run git config --list to verify everything is set correctly.

items.title: Basic Git Workflow
items.content:
This is the standard workflow you'll use 90% of the time with Git. Master this and you master version control.

Start with git init to create a repository. Make changes to your files, then use git status to see what changed. Stage changes with git add, then commit them with a message describing what you did.

Use git log to see the history of your commits. Connect to a remote repository with git remote add and push your changes with git push.

This workflow becomes second nature with practice. It's the foundation of all Git usage.
items.exercise: Create a project folder with mkdir myproject && cd myproject. Initialize Git with git init. Create a file with echo 'Hello Git' > readme.txt. Stage it with git add readme.txt. Commit it with git commit -m 'Initial commit'. View the history with git log --oneline.

items.title: Understanding Branches
items.content:
Branches let you work on different features separately. The main branch (often called main or master) is the stable version.

Create a new branch with git branch feature-name and switch to it with git checkout feature-name. Or do both at once with git checkout -b feature-name.

When your feature is ready, merge it back to main with git merge feature-name. Delete the branch with git branch -d feature-name when you're done.

Branches are one of Git's most powerful features, allowing multiple people to work on the same project without conflicts.
items.exercise: Create a new branch with git checkout -b feature-test. Make a change to your file. Switch back to main with git checkout main. Merge your changes with git merge feature-test. Delete the branch with git branch -d feature-test.

items.title: Working with GitHub
items.content:
Clone repositories to get code from GitHub and contribute to open source projects.

To clone a repository, use git clone https://github.com/user/repository.git. This downloads the entire repository to your device.

For SSH access, generate an SSH key with ssh-keygen -t ed25519, then add the public key to your GitHub account. This allows passwordless pushes and pulls.

Working with GitHub opens up a world of collaboration and access to open source projects.
items.exercise: Generate an SSH key with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'your@email.com'. View the public key with cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub. Add this key to your GitHub account under Settings > SSH and GPG keys. Then clone a public repository with git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git.

items.title: Undoing Changes
items.content:
Fix mistakes and revert changes in Git. There are several ways to undo depending on what you need.

To unstage a file (remove from staging but keep changes): git reset HEAD file.txt

To discard changes to a file (revert to last commit): git checkout -- file.txt

To undo the last commit (keep changes): git reset --soft HEAD~1

To undo the last commit (discard changes): git reset --hard HEAD~1

Understanding these undo commands gives you confidence to experiment and fix mistakes.
items.exercise: Make some commits, then practice undoing changes: unstage a file with git reset HEAD filename, discard changes with git checkout -- filename, and undo the last commit with git reset --soft HEAD~1. Each one works differently.

networking.title: Networking & SSH
networking.description: Connect to other computers and transfer files securely. SSH is the standard for remote access, and mastering it opens up a world of possibilities.

items.title: SSH Client
items.content:
SSH (Secure Shell) lets you securely connect to and control other computers. It's the standard for remote server access.

To connect, use ssh username@hostname_or_ip. For example, ssh user@192.168.1.100 connects to a computer on your local network.

Use -p to specify a different port (default is 22). Use -i to specify a private key file.

SSH is encrypted and secure, making it safe to use over the internet.
items.exercise: If you have another computer on your network, try connecting to it via SSH. For example: ssh user@192.168.1.100. If you don't have another computer, research how to set up a local SSH server for practice. Once connected, try running commands like ls or pwd.

items.title: SSH Server (Access Your Phone)
items.content:
Turn your phone into an SSH server and access it from your computer or another device.

Start the server with sshd. It runs on port 8022 (not 22, because Android restricts low ports).

Find your phone's IP address with ifconfig or ip addr show | grep inet. Then connect from your computer with ssh -p 8022 username@phone_ip.

You can make SSH start automatically by adding sshd to your .zshrc or .bashrc file.

Running an SSH server on your phone lets you access your files remotely and manage your device from any computer.
items.exercise: Start the SSH server on your phone with sshd. Find your phone's IP with ifconfig. Then from your computer, connect with ssh -p 8022 username@phone_ip (replace username and phone_ip with your actual username and IP). Once connected, try running commands on your phone from your computer.

items.title: File Transfer with SCP and Rsync
items.content:
SCP and Rsync use SSH to transfer files securely. SCP is simple and works like cp. Rsync is more efficient for large transfers.

SCP syntax: scp -P 8022 username@phone_ip:~/file.txt ./ copies from phone to computer.

Rsync is better for syncing folders: rsync -avz -e 'ssh -p 8022' username@phone_ip:~/documents/ ./backup/

SCP is good for single files, while Rsync is better for folders and large transfers because it only copies changed files.
items.exercise: Copy a file from your phone to your computer using SCP: scp -P 8022 username@phone_ip:~/file.txt ./. Then copy it back: scp localfile.txt username@phone_ip:~/. Then install rsync with pkg install rsync and sync a folder: rsync -avz -e 'ssh -p 8022' username@phone_ip:~/documents/ ./backup/

items.title: Network Tools
items.content:
Useful commands for testing connectivity and network diagnostics.

ping tests connectivity: ping google.com or ping -c 4 8.8.8.8.

wget and curl download files from the web. wget is simpler for downloads; curl is more flexible for APIs.

nmap scans for open ports. traceroute traces network paths. dig and nslookup perform DNS lookups.

These tools are essential for troubleshooting network issues and understanding how networks work.
items.exercise: Use ping to test connectivity to google.com: ping -c 4 google.com. Use curl to check your public IP: curl ifconfig.me. Use wget to download a small file: wget https://example.com/smallfile.txt. Try traceroute to see the path to google.com: traceroute google.com.

python-dev.title: Python Development
python-dev.description: Write and run Python code on your Android device. Python is one of the most popular languages for beginners and professionals alike.

items.title: Installing Python
items.content:
Python is a beginner-friendly programming language that's perfect for scripting and automation on Termux.

Install Python with pkg install python. Verify the installation with python --version.

Pip is Python's package manager. Upgrade it with pip install --upgrade pip.

You can run Python interactively with python (the REPL), or run a script with python my_script.py.

Python's simple syntax makes it ideal for learning programming and automating tasks.
items.exercise: Install Python with pkg install python. Verify it with python --version. Start the interactive interpreter with python, print 'Hello World' with print('Hello World'), and exit with exit(). Then create a file with echo "print('Hello from file')" > hello.py and run it with python hello.py.

items.title: Installing Python Packages
items.content:
Python has thousands of packages for everything from web development to data science. Use pip to install them.

Install a package with pip install package_name. You can install multiple packages at once.

List installed packages with pip list. Show details with pip show package_name.

Save your dependencies to a file with pip freeze > requirements.txt and install from that file with pip install -r requirements.txt.

Python packages extend what you can do with Python, from web scraping to machine learning.
items.exercise: Install the requests package with pip install requests. Then create a Python script with nano download.py that uses requests to download a webpage. Save it, run it with python download.py, and check the output. Then use pip freeze > requirements.txt to save your dependencies.

items.title: Creating a Simple Web Server
items.content:
Start a web server in one line of Python. This is great for sharing files or testing web development.

Use Python's built-in HTTP server: python -m http.server 8000. This serves the current directory on port 8000.

You can specify a different directory: python -m http.server 8000 --directory /sdcard/Download.

For more flexibility, use Flask: install it with pip install flask, then create a simple app.

Web servers built with Python are great for testing and sharing files on your local network.
items.exercise: Start a simple HTTP server with python -m http.server 8000. Open your browser and go to http://localhost:8000 to see your files. Press Ctrl+C to stop the server. Then try serving a specific directory with python -m http.server 8000 --directory /sdcard/Download.

node-dev.title: Node.js Development
node-dev.description: Build JavaScript applications with Node.js on Termux. Node.js is the runtime that powers modern web development.

items.title: Installing Node.js
items.content:
Node.js lets you run JavaScript outside of a browser. It's essential for modern web development and JavaScript tooling.

Install Node.js with pkg install nodejs. Verify with node --version and npm --version.

NPM is Node's package manager. You can run Node interactively with node (the REPL), or run a script with node app.js.

Node.js opens up JavaScript development on your phone, from web servers to command-line tools.
items.exercise: Install Node.js with pkg install nodejs. Verify it with node --version and npm --version. Start the REPL with node, type console.log('Hello'), and press Enter. Then exit with .exit. Create a file with echo "console.log('Hello from file')" > hello.js and run it with node hello.js.

items.title: Creating a Web Server with Express
items.content:
Express is the most popular Node.js web framework. It makes building web servers simple and fast.

Create a new project folder and initialize npm with npm init -y. Install Express with npm install express.

Create a server.js file with a basic Express server. Run it with node server.js or use nodemon for auto-restart.

Express is used by thousands of websites and is the foundation of many JavaScript web applications.
items.exercise: Create a project folder with mkdir myapp && cd myapp. Initialize npm with npm init -y. Install Express with npm install express. Create a server file that responds with 'Hello World'. Run it with node server.js and test it in your browser.

items.title: Useful npm Packages
items.content:
Install global tools and local packages for development. Global packages are installed with -g and are available everywhere.

Useful global packages: nodemon (auto-restart server), pm2 (process manager), npm-check (check outdated packages), http-server (simple HTTP server).

Local packages: axios (HTTP client), chalk (colored terminal output), dotenv (environment variables), commander (command line interfaces).

The npm ecosystem has packages for almost every need, making JavaScript development incredibly productive.
items.exercise: Install http-server globally with npm install -g http-server and use it to serve a directory with http-server. Install chalk locally in a project with npm install chalk and use it in a script to print colored output: console.log(chalk.blue('Hello')).

customization.title: Customization
customization.description: Make Termux look and feel the way you want. Customize your shell, colors, and shortcuts for a better experience.

items.title: Zsh and Oh My Zsh
items.content:
Upgrade from Bash to Zsh with themes and plugins. Zsh offers better auto-completion, theming, and plugins.

Install Zsh with pkg install zsh, then change your default shell with chsh -s zsh. Restart Termux for the change to take effect.

Install Oh My Zsh for easy theming: sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)". Change your theme by editing ~/.zshrc.

Zsh makes the terminal more user-friendly with features like better tab completion and beautiful prompts.
items.exercise: Install Zsh with pkg install zsh. Change your default shell with chsh -s zsh. Restart Termux. Then install Oh My Zsh with sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)". Change your theme by editing ~/.zshrc and setting ZSH_THEME='agnoster'. Apply changes with source ~/.zshrc.

items.title: Color Schemes
items.content:
Customize terminal colors by editing colors.properties. You can create your own theme or use a pre-made one.

Create the .termux directory if it doesn't exist: mkdir -p ~/.termux.

Edit colors.properties with nano ~/.termux/colors.properties. Add your color settings like background, foreground, cursor, and palette colors.

Restart Termux to apply your new color scheme.

Color schemes make the terminal more readable and can reduce eye strain.
items.exercise: Create a custom color scheme for your Termux. Create the directory with mkdir -p ~/.termux. Open colors.properties with nano ~/.termux/colors.properties. Add: background=black, foreground=white, cursor=purple. Save and restart Termux to see your changes.

items.title: Custom Aliases
items.content:
Create shortcuts for frequently used commands. Aliases save time and reduce typos.

Edit your shell configuration file (~/.zshrc for Zsh, ~/.bashrc for Bash). Add alias definitions like alias ll='ls -la'.

After adding aliases, reload your config with source ~/.zshrc (or source ~/.bashrc).

Common aliases: ll for ls -la, update for pkg update && pkg upgrade, home for cd ~.

Aliases can dramatically speed up your workflow by reducing keystrokes.
items.exercise: Add some useful aliases to your shell config: alias ll='ls -la', alias update='pkg update && pkg upgrade', alias home='cd ~'. Add them to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc. Reload your config with source ~/.zshrc (or source ~/.bashrc). Test your new aliases: ll, update, home.

shortcuts.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
shortcuts.description: Speed up your workflow with essential keyboard shortcuts. Learning shortcuts saves time and makes you more efficient.

items.title: Essential Terminal Shortcuts
items.content:
These shortcuts work in almost every terminal environment. Learn them to navigate and edit faster.

Ctrl+C stops the current process. Ctrl+D exits the current shell. Ctrl+L clears the screen.

Ctrl+A jumps to the beginning of the line, Ctrl+E jumps to the end. Ctrl+U deletes to the beginning, Ctrl+K deletes to the end.

Up/Down arrows navigate command history. Tab auto-completes commands and filenames.

These shortcuts work across all terminal environments, so learning them is a valuable skill.
items.exercise: Practice using each shortcut. Type a long command like echo 'this is a long command to practice editing'. Use Ctrl+A to go to the beginning, Ctrl+E to go to the end, Ctrl+U to delete to the beginning, and Ctrl+K to delete to the end. Then use Up arrow to recall the command and edit it again.

items.title: Termux-Specific Shortcuts
items.content:
Termux uses volume keys because Android keyboards lack certain keys like Ctrl, Alt, and Escape.

Volume Up + Q = Ctrl key. Volume Up + W = Tilde (~). Volume Up + E = Pipe (|). Volume Up + R = Backslash (\).

Volume Down + D = Escape key. Volume Down + L = Tab key. Volume Down + K = Delete key.

You can also add a permanent extra keys row with 'extra-keys' in termux.properties.

These shortcuts make it possible to access essential keys that aren't on your Android keyboard.
items.exercise: Try the volume key shortcuts: press Volume Up + Q to send Ctrl, Volume Up + E to type |, Volume Up + W to type ~. Then add an extra keys row with echo 'extra-keys = [["ESC","CTRL","ALT","LEFT","RIGHT","UP","DOWN"]]' > ~/.termux/termux.properties and reload with termux-reload-settings.

items.title: Nano Text Editor Shortcuts
items.content:
^ means Ctrl (so ^O means press Ctrl and O together). These shortcuts make editing in Nano fast and efficient.

^O saves the file (Write Out). ^X exits Nano. ^K cuts the current line. ^U pastes (Uncut) the cut line.

^W searches for text. ^\ searches and replaces. ^G shows help. ^C shows cursor position.

Alt+U undoes, Alt+E redoes. Alt+A selects text, Alt+6 copies the selected text.

Nano shortcuts are displayed at the bottom of the screen, making them easy to learn.
items.exercise: Open a file in Nano with nano test.txt. Practice saving with ^O, searching with ^W, cutting with ^K, and pasting with ^U. Then enable line numbers by creating ~/.nanorc with echo 'set linenumbers' >> ~/.nanorc. Open Nano again to see line numbers.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.description: Fix common issues and errors in Termux. Knowing how to troubleshoot saves time and frustration.

items.title: Repository Errors
items.content:
If pkg update fails, try these solutions.

First, change the repository mirror with termux-change-repo and select a different mirror.

If that doesn't work, clear the cache with pkg clean and try again. You can also reset repositories by removing the lists folder.

Check your internet connection with ping google.com and verify your date/time settings are correct.

Repository errors are usually caused by network issues or outdated mirrors.
items.exercise: Try changing your repository mirror using termux-change-repo to see the available options. Select a different mirror and see if pkg update works better. If not, clear the cache with pkg clean and try again.

items.title: Storage Permission Issues
items.content:
If you cannot access Android files, fix storage permissions.

Re-run termux-setup-storage to request permission again. Check Android Settings to ensure Termux has Storage permission.

On Android 11+, you may need to enable 'Allow management of all files' in the permissions settings.

You can also manually recreate the symlinks by removing ~/storage and running termux-setup-storage again.

Storage issues are often caused by permission changes or Android updates.
items.exercise: Check your storage permissions in Android Settings > Apps > Termux > Permissions. Make sure Storage is allowed. Then run termux-setup-storage again. If it still doesn't work, try rm -rf ~/storage && termux-setup-storage.

items.title: Package Installation Failures
items.content:
When pkg install fails, use these fixes.

First, update everything with pkg update && pkg upgrade. Then clear the cache with pkg clean.

Check your disk space with df -h — you might need to free up space. Try reinstalling the package with pkg reinstall <package>.

If dependencies are broken, run pkg install -f to fix them. Also verify that the package exists with pkg search <package-name>.

Most installation failures are due to network issues, disk space, or dependency problems.
items.exercise: Check your disk space with df -h. If you're low on space, clean the cache with pkg clean. Then try installing a package with pkg install <package>. If it fails, try pkg reinstall <package> or pkg install -f to fix dependencies.

items.title: SSH Connection Issues
items.content:
Fix problems when connecting via SSH.

First, check if sshd is running with ps aux | grep sshd. If not, start it with sshd.

Verify you're using the correct port (8022) and the correct IP address. Both devices must be on the same network.

Check permissions on ~/.ssh (should be 700) and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (should be 600).

Regenerate SSH keys if needed and check the SSH logs with logcat -s Termux:SSH.

SSH issues are usually caused by network configuration or permission problems.
items.exercise: Start sshd with sshd. Check if it's running with ps aux | grep sshd. Find your IP with ifconfig. Check SSH permissions with ls -la ~/.ssh. If permissions are wrong, fix them with chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Then try connecting from another device.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.description: Common questions and answers about Termux. Find answers to the most frequently asked questions.

items.title: Do I need root access?
items.content:
No. Termux works perfectly without root. The vast majority of features work without any root access at all.

Root access is only needed for certain advanced features like running root-only tools or modifying system files. For everyday use, learning, and development, root is not required.

Termux is designed to work on unrooted devices, and most users never need root.
items.exercise: Try using Termux without root — you'll find almost everything works perfectly. Install packages, create files, and run programs without any root access needed.

items.title: Play Store vs F-Droid?
items.content:
Always use the F-Droid version. The Play Store version is no longer maintained and has serious issues.

The Play Store version is years behind and broken. The F-Droid version is actively maintained, receives regular updates, and has all the latest features and security fixes.

Many users experience crashes and missing features with the Play Store version, which are all fixed in F-Droid.
items.exercise: Check which version you have installed by looking at the app details. If it's from Play Store, uninstall it and reinstall from F-Droid at https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.termux/.

items.title: How to update Termux?
items.content:
Termux itself is updated through F-Droid, not through the pkg command. Packages inside Termux are updated with pkg.

To update the Termux app itself, open F-Droid and go to Settings > Updates. Or download the latest APK from F-Droid.

To update packages inside Termux, run pkg update && pkg upgrade.

Keeping both the app and packages up to date ensures you have the latest features and security fixes.
items.exercise: Check your Termux version with pkg --version. Then check if there's an update available on F-Droid by opening F-Droid and looking for updates. If there's an update, install it. Then run pkg update && pkg upgrade to update your packages.

items.title: How to prevent Android from killing Termux?
items.content:
Android may terminate background apps to save battery. Here's how to prevent it.

Disable battery optimization for Termux in Android Settings. Use termux-wake-lock to keep Termux awake. Keep Termux in the foreground by running a long-running command.

You can also lock Termux in the recents view by opening the recent apps and tapping the lock icon.

These steps help ensure Termux stays running even when in the background.
items.exercise: Check your battery optimization settings for Termux: Settings > Apps > Termux > Battery > Unrestricted. Install termux-api with pkg install termux-api and use termux-wake-lock to keep Termux awake. Then lock Termux in recent apps by opening recent apps and tapping the lock icon.

items.title: Can I run GUI applications?
items.content:
Yes, you can run basic GUI applications using VNC or Termux:X11.

Termux:X11 is a native Android app that provides an X11 server for running GUI apps. You need to install it from F-Droid.

VNC is another option. Install tigervnc, start the server with vncserver, and connect with a VNC viewer app to localhost:5901.

Running GUI apps allows you to use graphical applications like text editors and development tools.
items.exercise: Install tigervnc with pkg install tigervnc. Start a VNC server with vncserver. Connect to it using a VNC viewer app on your phone or computer. Then install a GUI app like nano with pkg install nano and open it with export DISPLAY=:1 && nano.

items.title: How to change the default shell?
items.content:
The default shell is Bash. You can switch to Zsh for more features like better auto-completion and theming.

Install Zsh with pkg install zsh, then change your default shell with chsh -s zsh. Restart Termux for the change to take effect.

To change back to Bash, run chsh -s bash. You can see available shells with cat /etc/shells.

Zsh offers a more modern and feature-rich experience compared to Bash.
items.exercise: Install Zsh with pkg install zsh. Change your default shell with chsh -s zsh. Restart Termux. See available shells with cat /etc/shells. To change back to Bash, run chsh -s bash.

items.title: How to access Termux from PC without USB?
items.content:
Use SSH to access Termux remotely from your computer over WiFi.

On your phone, install openssh and start the server with sshd. Find your phone's IP address with ifconfig.

On your computer, connect with ssh -p 8022 username@phone_ip. Transfer files with scp -P 8022 file.txt username@phone_ip:~/

This is the most common way to access Termux remotely and is secure and fast.
items.exercise: Set up SSH on your phone: pkg install openssh, sshd. Find your IP with ifconfig. From your computer: ssh -p 8022 username@phone_ip. Then set up passwordless login: on your computer, generate an SSH key with ssh-keygen -t rsa, then copy it with ssh-copy-id -p 8022 username@phone_ip.
